title: Work schedule
description: An ordered plan over items a reconciliation left outstanding: waves of work whose dependencies are met, each wave named for the reason it exists rather than numbered, and every row carrying its own class, size and three-point range. A wave's name is load-bearing — 'nothing here can be trusted until this lands' is a scheduling constraint, and renumbering it into 'Wave 0' loses the constraint. Ranges are wide on purpose and must not be summed across waves that run concurrently, nor presented as a delivery date; `decided` records whether a person has actually agreed to this plan, and a schedule with `decided` false is a proposal being read as a commitment the moment somebody quotes its totals.

waves.description: The waves in execution order. Wave n assumes wave n-1 has landed; a wave whose members do not actually depend on the previous wave should be merged into it rather than kept for tidiness.

total_lo.description: Optimistic total across the plan, in minutes. Valid only under the concurrency the waves assume; it is not a delivery estimate.

total_hi.description: Pessimistic total, in minutes. The spread over `total_lo` is the honest uncertainty and compressing it is how a plan becomes a promise.

decided.description: Whether somebody with the authority to commit has actually agreed to this ordering. False means the file is a proposal — the ranges are real, the plan is not agreed, and a reader must label it so rather than presenting it as the schedule.

generated.description: When the plan was compiled. A schedule outlives the reconciliation it was built from and goes stale silently.

source.description: The reckon ledger or remaining-work file this plan was built from, so every row can be traced to the class that put it there.

n.description: Ordinal position, starting at 0 for work that must land before anything else can be trusted.

name.description: Why this wave exists, as a sentence. It carries the scheduling constraint that the ordinal cannot — that the wave's members share a cause, a risk, or a decision that has just been taken. Never replace it with a generic label.

members.description: Row count, carried so a truncated export is detectable.

wave_lo.description: Optimistic wall-clock minutes for the wave under the assumed concurrency.

wave_hi.description: Pessimistic wall-clock minutes for the wave.

blockers.description: Blocker ids that must lift before this wave can start.

note.description: Anything a scheduler needs that the numbers cannot carry.

id.description: The item's id in the tracker or ledger it came from. The join back to the evidence.

cls.description: The reconciliation class that put this row on the plan. The same closed eight-class partition the reckon ledger uses — see reckon-ledger.json. It matters here because `broken` and `unmeasured` are scheduled identically and mean opposite things: one is a product to fix, the other a check nobody has run, and a plan that loses the difference sends engineers to fix working software.

tier.description: Size class, in the same closed vocabulary the reckon ledger's estimates use.

title.description: The item, in the words of whoever raised it.

why.description: Why it is in THIS wave — the scheduling reason, not a restatement of the title. Where a person has ruled on it, the ruling goes here, because the ruling is the thing that changed and moved the row.

state.description: The tracker's current state for the item, verbatim, or a placeholder when the item has no tracker row. An OPEN vocabulary owned by the project's tracker.

hi.description: Pessimistic minutes. Ranges of 4-8x are normal for build work and are not a sign the estimate is bad.

flows.description: Journey ids this row returns to measurable, when known — what the work buys, expressed in the campaign's own currency.

owner.description: Who must act, when it is not the default owner of the wave.
